rv.q: If you have ever read a HARRY POTTER book or seen one of the films, you owe it to yourself to experience this one-of-a-kind staged phenomenon at least once.
Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Orpheum Theatre is a solid night out.
As a A.C. touring show when compared to a B.C. sit down show, I'd give this a MEH+.
To say it exceeded my expectations would be an understatement.
From the moment the show begins, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is FILLED with Hogwarts-level magic, bringing the wizarding world to life in a way that feels almost impossible.
Tiffany seamlessly guides the spirited cast, keeping the pace steady and allowing the wondrous special effects to transform The Fox into a showcase for theatricality.
It offers up so much theatrical magic that you won't be able to tear your eyes away from the stage.
“Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” offers a spellbinding saga, filled with incredible stage flair, otherworldly practical effects and, at times, unsettling pyrotechnics.
The production includes some of the most astonishing theatrical immersive magic ever seen on stage.
It's a joyous, at times agreeably jumbled experience that was worth the wait.
If you’re going for awe, wonder, and one of the most technically impressive stage experiences to hit Minneapolis, this production casts a powerful spell.
The spectacle’s the thing here, and all those parts shine quite well individually.
The show is enjoyable, fun and a decent companion to the series.

"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child," the Broadway touring production brought in by Zions Bank Broadway at the Eccles, offers magical live visual effects that seem to turn one character into another, spark fire battles with wizards' wands, and depict time travel between alternate realities.
Like I said, it is more a play to be enjoyed for the spectacle of it and the immersive experience rather than for the story or profundity of the message.

cn.t: Critics praise the touring production's spectacular stagecraft and visual effects, though many find the plot weak and convoluted. The show dazzles with technical wizardry even when the story doesn't quite cast its spell.
